report.answer_text:
Winners: Susumu Kitagawa of Kyoto University, Japan; Richard Robson of the University of Melbourne, Australia; and Omar M. Yaghi of the University of California, Berkeley, U.S.[1] The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the prize to the three equally "for the development of metal-organic frameworks."[1]
What they developed: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs). These are porous materials made of metal ions or clusters coordinated to organic linkers.[2] The many possible combinations of nodes and linkers allow MOFs to be designed with a wide range of structures and properties.[2]
Individual contributions:
Robson: He was among the first to design 3D structures by combining metal ions (such as copper) with organic molecules to form strong, interconnected frameworks.[3]
Yaghi: He coined the term "metal-organic frameworks" and developed reticular chemistry, a systematic approach to assembling metal ions and organic molecules into large, ordered structures.[3]
Kitagawa: I didn't find details of his specific contribution in these results.
Why it matters: The Nobel committee likened the structures to Hermione Granger's handbag from Harry Potter, small on the outside but very large on the inside.[4] Applications include gas storage, carbon capture, and water harvesting.[5] They can also be used for catalysis and capturing water from the air in arid regions.[6]
